## Race

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Race")]

### Start

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Start")]

Although the day started overcast, the race started in fine weather.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.44-21) Bucknum's Ford and Rodriguez's NART P3 were first away,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19) while both Chaparrals were among the last as [Jim Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hall_(racing_driver) "Jim Hall (racing driver)") insisted on his drivers doing up their full race-harness before leaving. At the end of the first lap it was the Mk IIBs of Bucknum and Gardner leading Gurney's MkIV, then the Ferraris of Rodriguez and Amon, and Surtees in the Lola. On the fourth lap the Lola's engine broke a piston. Spence meanwhile made great pace to work his way back up the field.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.44-21)

Early visitors to the pits included Hulme's Mk IV to fix a sticking throttle, Bianchi's Mk IV to check his windscreen after an errant stone cracked it and Gardner's Ford for a new front tyre.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.249-23) Dubois brought the Shelby Mustang in missing half its front spoiler after bumping fenders in the startline rush[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.256-24) and Jaussaud because his Matra's door wouldn't shut properly.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Automobile_Year_1967,_p.224-25) Bucknum continued to lead past the first hour, up to the first pitstops. After all the leaders had pitted, it was Foyt now leading from Hill in the Chaparral and the Fords of Andretti and McLaren with Parkes in 5th.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.243-26)

[![Image 185](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Porsche_907_%2847748356111%29.jpg/250px-Porsche_907_%2847748356111%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Porsche_907_(47748356111).jpg)

Porsche 907 LH of Mitter/Rindt, which retired after 9 hours. A similar 907 won the P2.0 class.

Suddenly Mike Salmon's JWA Ford GT burst into flames at over 300 km/h down the back straight with a full tank of fuel. Salmon bravely got the car near to a marshal post at Mulsanne corner before jumping out but was taken to hospital with severe 2nd and 3rd-degree burns.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.45-22) After two hours, the three Americans Foyt, Hill and Andretti (33 laps) already had a lap on the Ferraris and the rest of the field.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.45-22) After his early delay, Hulme then set a new lap record of 3:23.6, faster than the record pole time.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.45-22) The Ferraris were playing a long game, driving within their capability to last the distance. The Porsches of Siffert/Herrmann and Mitter/Rindt, now up to 14th and 15th overall, had a comfortable lead in the Index of Performance. However the big British cars were all out before dark: both the Mirages and the second Lola gone with engine issues after running outside the top-10.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clausager_1982,_p.153-1)

### Night

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Night")]

Soon after 10pm, as night was falling, Amon's Ferrari suffered a puncture while running 5th. Because of a faulty mallet he could not change the tyre out on the track[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19) and while crawling back to the pits, sparks from the wheel hub started a fire in the engine. Amon was forced to bail out quickly (unharmed) at a distance from any marshal posts and the car was burnt to a wreck.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.243-26) Not long later the Chaparral had to pit with its aileron stuck in the brake position, making the car lose about 20 km/h off its top speed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.109-111-3) Bucknum lost two hours to get a water-pipe rewelded then had to creep around for two laps to reach the mandatory 25-lap minimum for liquids replenishment[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19) Twice Lloyd Ruby ditched his Ford in the Mulsanne corner sandtrap, losing all the time Hulme had made up having to get repairs to the undertray. The second incident proved terminal.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19)

The Rodriguez/Baghetti NART Ferrari had slipped down the field and retired after 2am with a burnt piston. By 3am Ford was 1-2-3 with Gurney (182 laps) leading Andretti (who had recently matched Hulme's lap record) and McLaren by three laps. At 3:35 am, still running second, Andretti pitted J-7, the #3 Mk IV. A. J. Foyt, who had brought in J-5, the #1 Mk IV at the same time, was complaining loudly about his American rival's aggressive driving. Distracted by this “discussion,” a mechanic changing the front brake pads on J-7 installed a pad backward (which could be done). Andretti accelerated out of the pits and under the Dunlop bridge, but when he braked for the first time, from high speed going into the Esses, the incorrectly installed front brake locked, and J-7 spun, hitting the earth banks and ending up in disarray in the middle of the track.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-27) Andretti, with three broken ribs, leapt out and behind the wall. (It later transpired that Bianchi was right and the brakes had been put in back to front[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.244-6-7)) Soon behind him at speed came McCluskey (9th) who deliberately hit the other wall believing the wreck might still have the driver trapped inside, then Schlesser (6th) who tried to weave between the two. Both crashed and suddenly Ford were down three cars. McCluskey, carrying the injured Andretti, commandeered a marshal's car and drove back to the Ford medical centre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.244-6-7)

McLaren picked up a second puncture going through the debris, and then lost more time with clutch issues. To top it off, the rear engine bonnet later flew off racing down the Mulsanne straight and another 45 minutes were lost retrieving and refitting it, dropping them to 6th.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.243-26)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.39-41-19)

This left the Gurney/Foyt car with a 5-lap lead and elevated the Parkes/Scarfiotti Ferrari to second and the Hill/Spence Chaparral fighting back up to third. During the night, Gurney had eased off a little to preserve his car, and Parkes came up behind in the second-place Ferrari to unlap himself. For several miles Parkes hounded the Ford, flashing his lights in Gurney's mirrors until an exasperated Gurney simply pulled over at Arnage corner and stopped on a grass verge. Parkes stopped behind him, and the two race leaders sat there in the dark, motionless. Finally, Parkes conceded his attempt at provoking a race with Gurney was not going to work and he pulled out and resumed the race, with Gurney following shortly after. The Siffert/Herrmann Porsche still led the Index of Performance although it was now being chased by the improving Alpine of Larrousse/Depailler.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.46-28)

### Morning

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Morning")]

Dawn arrived clear and cold, with little mist this year.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.47-29) The Chaparral developed an oil-leak in the transmission dropping it down the order and then eventual retirement. The Belgian Ferrari P4 had been having a consistent race and slotted into third, with the other P4 of Klass/Sutcliffe now in fourth. However, a broken fuel-injection pump forced their retirement mid-morning.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.253-8) The Corvette retired with a broken conrod while leading the GT category.

Bucknum and Hawkins, early race-leaders, had driven hard to get back up to 6th after their overnight delay when they were finally halted by engine issues at 9.40am.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.244-6-7) So by 10am, the three-quarter mark, there were only 16 cars still running. Gurney and Foyt had already covered 293 laps, twenty more than McLaren and Amon had the previous year at the same time.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.47-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Automobile_Year_1967,_p.225-30) With a decent lead, the leading Ford could afford to drop its lap times by 30 seconds a lap. Even though the Ferraris were lapping 10 seconds a lap faster and could go 20% further between fuel-stops,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Automobile_Year_1967,_p.225-30) they were unable to make significant inroads, and the remaining quarter of the race was largely uneventful.

### Finish and post-race

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Finish and post-race")]

[![Image 186](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Alpinea210.jpg/250px-Alpinea210.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alpinea210.jpg)

Alpine A210 ofBianchi/Vinatier, which won the P 1.6 class 

In the end it was a comfortable victory for the all-American Ford with Gurney and Foyt winning by four laps, having led for all but the first 90 minutes of the race. Theirs was the only one of the ten Fords that did not have any issues throughout the race. Perhaps surprisingly for such a big engine, they also won the Index of Thermal Efficiency from their record distance covered. Ferrari salvaged some pride after the previous year's debacle with second and third, with McLaren/Donohue fighting back to fourth. As of 2026 this Gurney/Foyt victory remains both the only all-American victory in Le Mans history — American drivers ([Dan Gurney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Gurney "Dan Gurney") and [A. J. Foyt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._J._Foyt "A. J. Foyt")), team ([Shelby-American Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carroll_Shelby_International "Carroll Shelby International")), chassis constructor ([Ford USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company")), engine manufacturer (Ford), and tires ([Goodyear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodyear_Tire_and_Rubber_Company "Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company")) — as well as the only victory of a car designed and built entirely (both chassis and engine) in the United States.

Siffert and Herrmann were 5th in their new Porsche 907 2-litre, covering just 12 km less than the 1966 winners.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.109-111-3) They led home three more Porsche, the Stommelen/Neerpasch 910, and Pon/Elford in 7th being the first 906 Group 4 car home, surviving all of the GT40 Mk.I, while the other privateer Porsche 906 in 8th just beat the Alpine of Grandsire/Rosinski who won the 1300-class. The Swiss Ferrari GTB of Spoerry/Steinemann was the first GT home, coming 11th, nine laps ahead of the only French 911 that finished. The Austin-Healey, perennial finishers, was the only British car to make it to the end, in 15th.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Automobile_Year_1967,_p.232-31) The little Abarth, after a race bedevilled by issues, did finish (in last place) but had not completed enough laps to be classified, being a victim of the record performances of the leaders that had 5 times the engine capacity.

When the winners mounted the victory stand, Gurney was handed the traditional [magnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnum_(unit) "Magnum (unit)") of [champagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champagne "Champagne"). Looking down, he saw Ford CEO [Henry Ford II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford_II "Henry Ford II"), team owner [Carroll Shelby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carroll_Shelby "Carroll Shelby"), their wives, and several journalists who had predicted disaster for the high-profile duo of Gurney and Foyt. They had said that the two drivers, who were strongly competitive in the United States, would break their car in intramural rivalry. Instead, both drivers took special care to drive the car with discipline and won easily. On the victory stand, Gurney shook the bottle and sprayed everyone nearby, establishing a tradition re-enacted in victory celebrations the world over ever since.

> "What I did with the Champagne was totally spontaneous. I had no idea it would start a tradition. I was beyond caring and just got caught up in the moment. It was one of those once-in-a-lifetime occasions where things turned out perfectly... I thought this hard-fought victory needed something special”.

Gurney, incidentally, autographed and gave the bottle of champagne to _[Life Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life\_(magazine) "Life (magazine)")_ photographer, [Flip Schulke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flip_Schulke "Flip Schulke"), who used it as a lamp for 30 years. Schulke later returned the bottle to Gurney, who placed it in his [All American Racers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_American_Racers "All American Racers") team headquarters’ boardroom in California.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-33)

Chaparral got its due reward a month later with the only victory for the [2F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral_2F "Chaparral 2F") at Brands Hatch. It was a suitable finale for [Phil Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Hill "Phil Hill"), [1961 F1 World Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1961_Formula_One_season "1961 Formula One season") to retire from a distinguished sports-car racing career that included three Le Mans victories.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.258-11)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

34th 24 Hours of Le Mans endurance race

This article is about the race. For the 2019 film released internationally as _Le Mans '66_, see [_Ford v Ferrari_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_v_Ferrari "Ford v Ferrari").

1966 [24 Hours of Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "24 Hours of Le Mans")Previous: [1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "1965 24 Hours of Le Mans")Next: [1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "1967 24 Hours of Le Mans") Index: [Races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_races "Category:24 Hours of Le Mans races") | [Winners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_winners "List of 24 Hours of Le Mans winners")

The **1966 [24 Hours of Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "24 Hours of Le Mans")** was the 34th Grand Prix of Endurance, and took place on 18 and 19 June 1966.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-2) It was also the seventh round of the [1966 World Sportscar Championship season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_World_Sportscar_Championship_season "1966 World Sportscar Championship season"). This was the first overall win at Le Mans for the [Ford GT40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40 "Ford GT40") as well as the first win for an American constructor in a major European race since [Jimmy Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Murphy_(racing_driver) "Jimmy Murphy (racing driver)")'s triumph with [Duesenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duesenberg "Duesenberg") at the [1921 French Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1921_French_Grand_Prix "1921 French Grand Prix").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Sauber-3) It was also the debut Le Mans start for two significant drivers: [Henri Pescarolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Pescarolo "Henri Pescarolo"), who went on to set the record for the most starts at Le Mans; and [Jacky Ickx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacky_Ickx "Jacky Ickx"), whose record of six Le Mans victories stood until beaten by [Tom Kristensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kristensen_(racing_driver) "Tom Kristensen (racing driver)") in 2005.

## Regulations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Regulations")]

The year 1966 saw the advent of a completely new set of regulations from the CSI (Commission Sportive Internationale – the [FIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Internationale_de_l'Automobile "Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile")'s regulations body) – the FIA Appendix J, redefining the categories of motorsport in a numerical list. GT cars were now [Group 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_3_(racing) "Group 3 (racing)") and Prototypes were now [Group 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_6_(racing) "Group 6 (racing)"), Sports Cars were still [Group 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_4_(racing) "Group 4 (racing)") and Special Touring Cars was a new category defined by [Group 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_5_(racing) "Group 5 (racing)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-4) (Group 1 and 2 covered other Touring Cars, [Group 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_7_(racing) "Group 7 (racing)") led to the [Can-Am series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Can-Am_season "1966 Can-Am season"), with Group 8 and 9 for single-seaters).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.208-5)

As Group 7 were ineligible for FIA championship events, the [Automobile Club de l'Ouest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile_Club_de_l'Ouest "Automobile Club de l'Ouest") (ACO) opened its entry list to Group 3, 4 and 6. The FIA mandated minimum annual production runs of 500 cars for Group 3 (up from 100 previously[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clausager_1982,_p.140-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.102-4-7)) and 50 for Group 4,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.102-4-7) which also had a maximum engine capacity of 5000cc. There were no engine limits on the GTs or Prototypes. As before, the Groups were split up in classes based on engine size, there was a sliding scale of a minimum weight based on the increasing engine size (from 450 to 1000 kg for 500 to 7000cc) as was fuel-tank capacity (60 to 160 litres).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.208-5)

Along with the new Appendix J, after four years of focus on GT racing the FIA announced the International Manufacturer's Championship, for Group 6 Prototypes (2L / >2L), and the International Sports Car Championship for Group 4 (1.3L / 2L / 5L).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.208-5)

With the new regulations this year the ACO received a huge 103 entry requests. Such was the interest in Group 6 there were 43 prototypes on the starting grid and only 3 GT cars:

| Category | Classes | Prototype Group 6 | Sportscar Group 4 | GT Group 3 | Total entries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Large-engines | 2.0 - 7.0L | 21 | 5 (+3 reserve) | 1 (+1 reserve) | 27 (+4 reserves) |
| Medium-engines | 1.6 - 2.0L | 12 | 1 (+1 reserve) | 2 | 15 (+1 reserve) |
| Small-engines | 1.0 - 1.3L | 13 (+2 reserves) | 0 | 0 | 13 (+2 reserves) |
| Total cars |  | 46 (+2 reserves) | 6 (+4 reserves) | 3 (+1 reserve) | 55 (+7 reserves) |

After 2 years of its 3-year program, [Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company") had very little to show for its immense investment. From the 1966 season onwards, the GT40 could race in two categories. The standard 4.7-litre Mk.I had been homologated in the new Group 4 Sportscars 5.0 class, to let customers teams compete mainly with older 3.3 litre [Ferrari 250 LM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari_250_LM "Ferrari 250 LM"). For the big prototype class, and overall wins, the factory Mk.II was developed. Extensive work was done in the wind tunnel, and improving the brakes, handling and engine – not least improving the fuel economy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.6-7-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.201-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.18-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.209-11) The 7-litre Ford [NASCAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASCAR "NASCAR") race engine now put out ca. 550 bhp but was registered as "485 hp" as a result of Ford's lowered rev-limit setting for the 24h race.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.102-4-7) The new year started with promise with [Ken Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Miles "Ken Miles") and [Lloyd Ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Ruby "Lloyd Ruby") winning both the inaugural [24 Hours of Daytona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_of_Daytona "24 Hours of Daytona"), and then [12 Hours of Sebring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12_Hours_of_Sebring "12 Hours of Sebring").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.201-9) Copying [Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari "Ferrari")'s tactic of overwhelming numbers, they put in fifteen Mark II entries; eight were accepted by the ACO, plus five Mk.I in Gr. 4 Sportscars 5.0 class. This time six Mk. II were built and prepared by [Holman & Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holman_Moody "Holman Moody"). [Shelby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelby_American "Shelby American") ran three cars for Americans [Dan Gurney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Gurney "Dan Gurney") and [Jerry Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Grant "Jerry Grant"), Miles was now paired with New Zealander [Denny Hulme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denny_Hulme "Denny Hulme") after Ruby had been injured in a plane crash a month earlier.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.198-12) The third car was the all-[Kiwi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwi_(people) "Kiwi (people)") pairing of [Bruce McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_McLaren "Bruce McLaren") and [Chris Amon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Amon "Chris Amon"). Holman & Moody, the successful Ford NASCAR race team also brought another trio of GT40s as backups, – for [Mark Donohue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Donohue "Mark Donohue")/[Paul Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hawkins_(racing_driver) "Paul Hawkins (racing driver)"), [Ronnie Bucknum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Bucknum "Ronnie Bucknum")/[Dick Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Hutcherson "Dick Hutcherson"), and [Lucien Bianchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Bianchi "Lucien Bianchi")/[Mario Andretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Andretti "Mario Andretti").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.15-13) One of the big improvements Holman & Moody brought with them was a quick-change brake pad system to save time in the pits.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.21-14)

The British team [Alan Mann Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Mann_Racing "Alan Mann Racing") had two Mk.II cars prepared by Ford Advanced Vehicles, for [Graham Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Hill "Graham Hill")/[Dick Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Thompson_(racing_driver) "Dick Thompson (racing driver)") and [John Whitmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Whitmore_(racing_driver) "John Whitmore (racing driver)")/[Frank Gardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gardner_(racing_driver) "Frank Gardner (racing driver)"). Each of the eight cars was painted in a colour from the [Mustang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Mustang_(first_generation) "Ford Mustang (first generation)") road-car range.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.10-16)

Ferrari's response to the Mk II was the new [Ferrari 330 P3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari_P#330_P3 "Ferrari P"). Shorter and wider than the P2, it kept the same 4-litre engine but with fuel-injection now put out 420 bhp.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.209-11) The works team had a pair of closed-cockpit versions for [John Surtees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surtees "John Surtees")/[Ludovico Scarfiotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovico_Scarfiotti "Ludovico Scarfiotti") and former winners [Lorenzo Bandini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_Bandini "Lorenzo Bandini")/[Jean Guichet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Guichet "Jean Guichet"). An open-cockpit variant was given to the [North American Racing Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Racing_Team "North American Racing Team") (NART) for [Pedro Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Rodriguez_(racing_driver) "Pedro Rodriguez (racing driver)")/[Richie Ginther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richie_Ginther "Richie Ginther"). But their race preparation had been limited by strike action in Italy.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.217-9-17)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.201-9)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Laban_2001,_p.150-1-18)

NART also entered a long-tailed P2, rebodied by [Piero Drogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piero_Drogo "Piero Drogo") and driven by last year's winner [Masten Gregory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masten_Gregory "Masten Gregory") with [Bob Bondurant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Bondurant "Bob Bondurant"). There were also P2/P3 hybrids for the [Ecurie Francorchamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecurie_Francorchamps "Ecurie Francorchamps") (Dumay/"Beurlys") and [Scuderia Filipinetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuderia_Filipinetti "Scuderia Filipinetti") ([Mairesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Mairesse "Willy Mairesse")/[Müller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_M%C3%BCller_(racing_driver) "Herbert Müller (racing driver)")). Finally there was a P2 Spyder for Maranello Concessionaires ([Attwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Attwood "Richard Attwood")/[Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Piper_(racing_driver) "David Piper (racing driver)")).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.217-9-17)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.9-19) Fighting on two fronts, the company also took on the new [Porsche 906](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche_906 "Porsche 906") in the 2-litre prototype class with its [Dino 206 S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dino_206_S "Dino 206 S") with a pair from NART, and another for Maranello. [Nino Vaccarella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nino_Vaccarella "Nino Vaccarella"), race winner in [1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "1964 24 Hours of Le Mans"), was furious when he found out he was ‘demoted’ to drive the Dino rather than the P3 and threatened to walk out, but did, in the end run the car.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.24-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21)

[Chevrolet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet "Chevrolet") as engine supplier was the other player in the over 2-litre class. Ex-Ferrari engineer [Giotto Bizzarrini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giotto_Bizzarrini "Giotto Bizzarrini") had fallen out with [Renzo Rivolta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renzo_Rivolta "Renzo Rivolta") and with his own company brought his new design, the P538, but still using the 5.3L Chevrolet engine. The other Chevy was in Texan [Jim Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hall_(racing_driver) "Jim Hall (racing driver)")'s [Chaparral 2D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral_Cars#2 "Chaparral Cars"). The 5.3L small block put out 420 bhp and had a semi-automatic transmission.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Laban_2001,_p.150-1-18)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.102-4-7) Driven by [Phil Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Hill "Phil Hill") and [Jo Bonnier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Bonnier "Jo Bonnier"), they made a big impact winning the [1000km Nürburgring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000km_N%C3%BCrburgring "1000km Nürburgring") round just two weeks earlier.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.227-22)

[Porsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche "Porsche") came with a new model – the _[Porsche 906](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche\_906 "Porsche 906") Carrera 6_ designed by the team led by [Ferdinand Piëch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Pi%C3%ABch "Ferdinand Piëch"). With the 2.0L flat-6 engine from the 911 replacing the F4 of the _[Porsche 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche\_904 "Porsche 904") Carrera GTS_, and carrying over some parts of the two-year-old design, it was intended mainly for sale to customers racing for Sportcars class wins. By May 1966 it was homologated for Group 4 as the requisite 50 cars were made.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.210-23) The standard model was race-proven too, after winning the [1966 Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Targa_Florio "1966 Targa Florio") the month before after the prototype version were crashed by infighting pilots. Three cars were entered in the S 2.0 class where no opposition showed up as the Ferrari [Dino 206 S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dino_206_S "Dino 206 S") never was homologated, and older models from Alfa, Lotus etc. were inferior. In the P 2.0 prototype class, modifications were permitted, but the fuel-injected 906E was absent. Three regular carburettor engine prototypes fitted with "langheck" (long-tail) bodies were entered by the works team, driven by [Hans Herrmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Herrmann "Hans Herrmann")/[Herbert Linge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Linge "Herbert Linge"), [Jo Siffert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Siffert "Jo Siffert")/[Colin Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Davis_(racing_driver) "Colin Davis (racing driver)") and [Udo Schütz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udo_Sch%C3%BCtz "Udo Schütz")/[Peter de Klerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_de_Klerk "Peter de Klerk").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.220-1-24)

[Alfa Romeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo "Alfa Romeo"), and its works team [Autodelta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autodelta "Autodelta"), had withdrawn from racing for a year to prepare a new car for 1967.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.6-7-8) But this year, a significant new manufacturer entered the fray: [Matra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matra "Matra") had bought out [Automobiles René Bonnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobiles_Ren%C3%A9_Bonnet "Automobiles René Bonnet") in 1964, rebadging the [Djet as Matra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matra_Djet "Matra Djet"). However it was a new design that was entered as prototype. Formula One had "returned to power", doubling engine size from 1500cc in 1965 to 3000cc in 1966. The [BRM V8 Formula 1 engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRM_V8_engine "BRM V8 engine") could only be enlarged to approx. 2.1 litre, not enough for current F1, thus it was moved to endurance racing. The M620 had a 1.9-litre version of the [BRM V8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRM_V8_engine "BRM V8 engine") Formula 1 engine developing 245 bhp that could match the Porsches in speed, making 275 kp/h (170 mph). The three cars were driven by up and coming young French single-seater drivers [Jean-Pierre Beltoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Beltoise "Jean-Pierre Beltoise")/[Johnny Servoz-Gavin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Servoz-Gavin "Johnny Servoz-Gavin"), [Jean-Pierre Jaussaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Jaussaud "Jean-Pierre Jaussaud")/[Henri Pescarolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Pescarolo "Henri Pescarolo"), and [Jo Schlesser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Schlesser "Jo Schlesser"), with Welshman [Alan Rees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Rees_(racing_driver) "Alan Rees (racing driver)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.222-25)

Remarkably, given British dominance of the race barely a decade earlier, there were only three British cars in this year's race. Defending class-champions Austin-Healey had two works entries. The other was a [Marcos Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcos_Engineering "Marcos Engineering") kit-car based on a Mini Cooper 'S' chassis. Entered by Frenchman Hubert Giraud and driven by Jean-Louis Marnat and [Claude Ballot-Léna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Ballot-L%C3%A9na "Claude Ballot-Léna"), the team was able to get a works engine and gearbox from [BMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Motor_Corporation "British Motor Corporation"). The spectators laughed at the small car and its apparent resemblance to a flea.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.233-26) But the Mini Marcos would become the 'darling of the crowds' later on in the race.

[Alpine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobiles_Alpine "Automobiles Alpine"), after its poor showing in the previous year, returned with 6 cars. The new A210 had a 1.3L [Gordini-Renault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordini "Gordini") engine with a Porsche gearbox making it more durable if only a little faster at 245 kp/h (150 mph). This year a new customer team, the Ecurie Savin-Calberson was supported by Alpine, with former Index winner Roger Delageneste.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.224-27)

[Charles Deutsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Deutsch "Charles Deutsch") (CD) brought his new aerodynamic SP66. The car was powered by a 1130cc [Peugeot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peugeot "Peugeot") engine, marking the return of the French company last seen in the 1938 race.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.231-28) Another competitor in the small prototypes was [ASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASA_(automobile) "ASA (automobile)"). Originally a Ferrari design by [Carlo Chiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Chiti "Carlo Chiti") and [Giotto Bizzarrini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giotto_Bizzarrini "Giotto Bizzarrini") before their famous [walk-out from Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Ferrari#1961_%E2%80%93_The_great_walkout "History of Ferrari"), it was sold to the new Italian company and uprated with a 1290cc engine giving 125 bhp. Two cars were entered, one by ASA and one by NART.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.228-29)

The new Group 4 Sportscar category started attracting interest as the earlier prototypes were meeting the homologation and production requirements. There were six [Ford GT40 Mk.I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40_Mk.I "Ford GT40 Mk.I") entered by customer teams, with the 4.7L engine. [Jochen Rindt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jochen_Rindt "Jochen Rindt"), the previous year's winner in a then-prototype [Ferrari 250 LM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari_250_LM "Ferrari 250 LM") that was now eligible as Gr.4 S 5.0, had moved across from Ferrari to Ford, in the new Canadian Comstock Racing Team. They joined [Ford France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_France "Ford France"), [Scuderia Filipinetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuderia_Filipinetti "Scuderia Filipinetti") and new privateers Scuderia Bear and [Essex Wire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_Essex "Superior Essex"). Joining Skip Scott, team owner of the Essex Wire team, was a 21-year old [Jacky Ickx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacky_Ickx "Jacky Ickx") in his Le Mans debut.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.214-5-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clausager_1982,_p.147-31)

Up against them was [Ed Hugus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Hugus "Ed Hugus")’ modified Ferrari 275 GTB and the [Equipe Nationale Belge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecurie_Nationale_Belge "Ecurie Nationale Belge") ran its 250 LM. Porsche also ran three regular [Porsche 906](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche_906 "Porsche 906") unopposed in the Sports 2.0 category, two works entries as well as one for their Paris importer _Sonauto_ of [Toto Veuillet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Veuillet "Auguste Veuillet").

With Shelby now fully concentrated on the Ford GT40 Mk. II program, the Cobra GTs were abandoned. There were only three GT entries: the Ferrari customer teams [Écurie Francorchamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89curie_Francorchamps "Écurie Francorchamps") and [Maranello Concessionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maranello_Concessionaires?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maranello Concessionaires (page does not exist)") both entered a [Ferrari 275 GTB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari_275_GTB "Ferrari 275 GTB"). The third was a quiet though significant entry: Jacques Dewes, ever the pioneering privateer, brought the first [Porsche 911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche_911_(classic) "Porsche 911 (classic)") to Le Mans. Production of what would become the ubiquitous Le Mans car had started in late 1964, and along with the development of similar engine in the [Porsche 906](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche_906 "Porsche 906"), the new 1967 911 S model had its 2.0 litre ‘boxer’ flat-6-cylinder tuned to 160 bhp.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.223-32)

Finally, in a sub competition of its own, there was the tire race between [Firestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Tire_and_Rubber_Company "Firestone Tire and Rubber Company"), [Dunlop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunlop_Tyres "Dunlop Tyres"), and [Goodyear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodyear_Tire_and_Rubber_Company "Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.6-7-8)

## Test weekend

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Test weekend")]

Once again there was rain at the April testing weekend. And once again there was tragedy with a fatal accident. American Walt Hansgen's Ford hit water on the pit straight and aquaplaned. He aimed for the escape road at the end of the straight, not realising it was blocked by a sandbank, which he hit at about 190 km/h (120 mph). Taken with critical injuries to the American military hospital at [Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orl%C3%A9ans "Orléans"), he died five days later.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.198-12)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21)

A notable absentee at the test weekend was the Ferrari works team.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.6-7-8)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) Chris Amon was fastest at the test weekend in the experimental [Ford J-car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40#J-car "Ford GT40") with a 3:34.4 lap.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.102-4-7)

## Practice

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Practice")]

Come race-week it was Gurney who put in the fastest qualifying lap of 3:30.6, a second faster than his stablemates Miles, Gardner and McLaren. Ginther was 5th in the fastest Ferrari with a 3:33.0, with Parkes and Bandini in 7th and 8th respectively. Phil Hill, in the Chaparral, broke up the Ford-Ferrari procession in 10th.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.235-33)

In the 2.0 litre classes, Jo Siffert put the quickest Porsche 22nd on the grid with 3:51.0, with Nino Vaccarella's Ferrari Dino in 24th (3:53.5) and Jo Schlesser's Matra just behind it (3:53.5). Over the test weekend, Mauro Bianchi had surprised many in the 1-litre Alpine, going as fast as the 1959 Ferrari Testa Rossas.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.224-27)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) The quickest Alpine in practice was [Toivonen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauli_Toivonen "Pauli Toivonen")/Jansson (4:20.1), well ahead of the best CD (Ogier/Laurent 4:27.5) and the Austin-Healey's (4:45.1) and ASAs (4:49.8).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.235-33)

There were also two significant dramas in practice. The biggest news was the walkout of Ferrari's lead driver [John Surtees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surtees "John Surtees"). He and team manager Eugenio Dragoni had decided that he, as the fastest Ferrari driver and driving with [Mike Parkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Parkes "Mike Parkes"), would act as the hare to bait and break the Fords. He was also still recovering from a big accident the previous year and would hand over to Scarfiotti if he got overly tired. Yet during raceweek, with news that new FIAT chairman [Gianni Agnelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Agnelli "Gianni Agnelli") would be at the race, Dragoni changed the plan, putting Agnelli's nephew Scarfiotti in first, a case of [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism"). Surtees was furious and stormed off to Maranello to argue his case with [Enzo Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Ferrari "Enzo Ferrari").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) Not listened to, Surtees, Ferrari's [1964 F1 World Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Formula_One_season "1964 Formula One season"), quit the team.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.217-9-17)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.9-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.24-20)

The second incident was more serious – Dick Thompson in the Alan Mann Ford Mk II collided with Dick Holqvist who was going far slower in the Scuderia Bear Ford GT40 Mk.I and pulled right in front of him at Maison Blanche.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.9-19) Holqvist spun off with heavy damage, while Thompson was able to get back to the pits. While repairing the damage, officials told the team that they were disqualified for Thompson leaving the scene of a major accident. Thompson was adamant he had advised pit officials, and in the hearing Ford's director of racing Leo Beebe threatened to withdraw all Fords. He was supported by [Huschke von Hanstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Huschke_von_Hanstein "Fritz Huschke von Hanstein") who was prepared to withdraw the Porsche team as well.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) In the end, the car was reinstated though Thompson was banned. This still posed a problem for Ford as they were lacking spare drivers for their fleet of entries, with injuries to [A. J. Foyt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._J._Foyt "A. J. Foyt") (fire crash at [June 1966 Milwaukee Mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IndyCar_Series_at_the_Milwaukee_Mile "IndyCar Series at the Milwaukee Mile")), [Jackie Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Stewart "Jackie Stewart") (crashed at the [1966 Belgian Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Belgian_Grand_Prix "1966 Belgian Grand Prix")) and [Lloyd Ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Ruby "Lloyd Ruby") (spinal injuries in a plane crash).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.9-19) In the end Australian [Brian Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Muir_(racing_driver) "Brian Muir (racing driver)"), who was in England, was flown over to France. He did his two laps, his first ever at Le Mans, on raceday morning to qualify.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.214-5-30)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.10-16)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.24-20)

## Race

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Race")]

### Start

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Start")]

American businessman [Henry Ford II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford_II "Henry Ford II") was the honorary starter.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) Last-minute rain resulted in tire changes and some cars switched from Firestone to Goodyear or Dunlop.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.10-16)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.24-20) At the end of the first lap Ford's cars led – Hill ahead of Gurney then Bucknum, Parkes in the Ferrari, followed by Whitmore's Ford, the Chaparral, then the GT40s of Scott and Rindt.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.10-16) There had been instant excitement when Edgar Berney spun his Bizzarrini on the start-line amongst the crowd of departing cars.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.232-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clausager_1982,_p.144-35)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) Miles had to pit after the first lap to fix his door because earlier, he had slammed the door on his helmet. Also pitting on the first lap was Paul Hawkins whose Ford broke a halfshaft going down the [Mulsanne Straight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulsanne_Straight "Mulsanne Straight") lurching him sideways at nearly 350 km/h.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.10-16) The Holman & Moody crew took 70 minutes to repair it only for Mark Donohue to have the rear boot blow off down the Mulsanne and find the differential had been terminally damaged.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.10-16)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.25-36)

On the third lap Gurney took the lead, which he held onto until the first pit-stops. McLaren was being delayed by his tires going off, so the team quietly changed from Firestones to Goodyears.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15) After only 9 laps, Rindt's Ford blew its engine at the end of the Mulsanne straight, so there would be no consecutive win.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.214-5-30) At the end of the first hour Fords were 1-2-3, with Gurney leading by 24 seconds from Graham Hill and Bucknum. Fourth, 20 seconds further back, was the first NART Ferrari, of Rodriguez. Meanwhile, Miles had been putting in extremely fast laps, breaking the lap record and getting back up to 5th place. Parkes was 6th ahead of Bonnier in the Chaparral who had already been lapped. Within another hour Miles and Hulme had taken the lead.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.208-9-37)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.201-9)

At 8pm, only the Miles and Gurney Fords and Rodriguez's Ferrari were on the lead lap (#64).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.26-38) At dusk it started to drizzle, reducing the power advantage of the big Fords, and allowing the Ferraris to keep in touch. The Fords were further delayed as a number chose to change brake pads early.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.208-9-37) By then all three Dinos were out with mechanical issues, removing one threat to Porsche.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Armstrong_1966,_p.235-21) A major accident occurred when Jean-Claude Ogier's CD got loose on spilt oil at the Mulsanne kink and was hit hard side-on by François Pasquier in the NART ASA. Both cars hit the wall and caught fire, and Ogier was taken to the hospital with two broken arms.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.228-29)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.231-28)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.11-39)

### Night

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Night")]

After 6 hours, heavy rain was pouring down. Ginther's NART Ferrari was leading from Parkes, chased by the Fords of Miles and Gurney on the same lap, McLaren a lap behind, then Bandini and Andretti two laps back. But Andretti was soon sidelined with a blown headgasket, as was the Hill/Muir Ford which had broken its front suspension coming out of Arnage corner.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.12-40) As the rain eased, the Fords of Miles and Gurney retook the lead. Just before midnight [Robert Buchet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Buchet "Robert Buchet") aquaplaned coming over the crest at the Dunlop Bridge and crashed the French Porsche.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.220-1-24) The Chaparral had been running well initially, getting as high as 5th, until a broken alternator stopped them also just before midnight while running in 8th.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.227-22)

[![Image 9: The aftermath of the nighttime accident at the Esses, which resulted in the retirement of cars 20, 34, 42, and 53.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_crash_%284771648222%29.jpg/250px-1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_crash_%284771648222%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_crash_(4771648222).jpg)

The aftermath of the nighttime accident at the Esses which resulted in the retirement of cars #20, #34, #42, and #53.

Another heavy downpour at 12.30 contributed to a big accident in the Esses. Guichet had just spun his Ferrari in the rain and got away when Buchet arrived and crashed his Porsche. Then Schlesser's Matra ran into the CD of Georges Heligouin avoiding the accident. As the damage was being cleared, Scarfiotti crashed his P3 into the Matra and all four cars were wrecked, although only Scarfiotti was taken to hospital, with minor bruising.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.208-9-37)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.11-39)

[![Image 10: The Ferrari 330 P3 of Bandini/Guichet, which retired after 17 hours.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_21_%284771041799%29.jpg/250px-1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_21_%284771041799%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_21_(4771041799).jpg)

The Ferrari 330 P3 of Bandini/Guichet, which retired after 17 hours.

During the night the Ferraris started to suffer from overheating. When the NART P3 retired from 4th with a broken gearbox at 3am, and the Filipinetti car of Mairesse/Müller from 5th an hour later, the Ferrari challenge was spent – there would be no privateer-saviours for the marque this year. At halfway, Ford GT40s held the first 6 places: the Mk IIs held the top-4 places (Miles/Hulme, Gurney/Grant, McLaren/Amon, Bucknum/Hutcherson) with the Mk Is in 5-6-8: Essex, Filipinetti and Ford-France (Revson/Scott, Spoerry/Sutcliffe, Ligier/Grossman). Siffert/Davis were leading a train of Porsches in 7th and the nearest Ferrari was the Bandini/Guichet P3 limping in 12th. Ford told their cars to drop to 4-minute laps, but Gurney and Miles kept racing hard for the lead.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.12-40)

### Morning

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Morning")]

[![Image 11: The #2 GT40 of McLaren/Amon passes the wrecked #14 GT40 of Spoerry/Sutcliffe at the Esses.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_2_%284770959219%29.jpg/250px-1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_2_%284770959219%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_2_(4770959219).jpg)

The #2 GT40 of McLaren/Amon passes the wrecked #14 GT40 of Spoerry/Sutcliffe at the Esses.

What could have been a procession was anything but for Ford. At 8 am, a pit-stop for the Filipinetti Ford running 5th spilled petrol on a rear tyre. On his out-lap Spoerry lost traction and spun at the Esses wrecking the car. The [Ford France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_France "Ford France") and Essex cars had already retired with engine issues during the night.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.214-5-30)

At 9am the Gurney/Grant car, which had been dicing for the lead with Miles & Hulme (against strict team orders), retired from 1st when the car blew a headgasket. That left Ford with only three Mk IIs left (albeit running 1-2-3) as all the GT40 Mk Is had retired as well. Porsches now held the next five places and the two Ferrari GTs were 9th and 10th chased by the Alpines.

### Three Ford "photo" finish - ACO declares winner

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Three Ford \"photo\" finish - ACO declares winner")]

At about the 6 hour mark (to the finish) it was clear that Miles / Hulme and McLaren/Amon were set to win, a "PR" plan was developed to have all three Ford cars cross the finish line together to thus commemorate the historical first Ford / USA victory at Le Mans.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Petersen_Automotive_Museum-41) The notion was supported by Carrol Shelby as a means to totally "beat" Ferrari.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-youtube.com-42)

[![Image 12: The GT40 of Miles/Hulme, who finished 2nd overall.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_1_%284771000677%29.jpg/250px-1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_1_%284771000677%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_1_(4771000677).jpg)

The GT40 of Miles/Hulme, who finished 2nd overall

At the 3 hour mark during the last driver change (Amon to McLaren) and (Hulme to Miles), Miles was directly instructed to slow down and allow McLaren to catch up to allow for a "dead heat finish". Miles and his crew team were upset but agreed. Accordingly, on the final lap the next car from Ford driven by Bruce McLaren/[Chris Amon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Amon "Chris Amon") and the third-place car from Ford drew up, and they cruised to the line together.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-43) Miles's #1 car and McLaren's #2 car crossed the finish line almost at the same time, with photos and official track data showing McLaren's #2 as 6 metres ahead when crossing the line.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Data-45) Additionally, McLaren's #2 started just over 14 metres behind Miles's car and had therefore covered more distance during the race; the official rules regarding cars finishing together indicate that starting position should be taken into account, so McLaren was declared the winner.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clarke_1997,_p.13-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-:3-47)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Data-45)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Petersen_Automotive_Museum-41)

This was all unbeknownst to the Ford team. They were under the impression that Miles had "won" the race, but McLaren was indeed declared the 1966 Le Mans winner. In a 1997 interview Shelby lamented the ACO "made up rule" and that indeed "Ken Miles won the race" and feelings of guilt about what had occurred.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-youtube.com-42)

[![Image 13: The Porsche 908 of Siffert/Davis, which finished 4th OA, won the 2.0 liter prototype class and claimed the index of performance.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_30_%284770995759%29.jpg/250px-1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_30_%284770995759%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_30_(4770995759).jpg)

The Porsche 906/6 LH of Siffert/Davis, which finished 4th overall, won the 2.0 liter prototype class and claimed the index of performance.

At their last pitstop, the 7th-placed Gr.4 Porsche of [Peter Gregg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gregg_(racing_driver) "Peter Gregg (racing driver)") and Sten Axelsson was stopped by engine problems. Gregg parked the car waiting for the last lap, but at 3.50pm he could not get it restarted, missed the formation finish and was DNF. The other four Porsches came in 4th to 7th led by Siffert/Davis, who also claimed the Index of Performance. The [Stommelen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolf_Stommelen "Rolf Stommelen")/[Klass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Klass "Günter Klass") car in 7th was the first, and only, Sports car to finish, beating all Mk.I and Ferrari. Finally, the new 911S GT car ran well and finished 14th starting a long record of success.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.220-1-24)

Four Alpines finished this year, 9-11-12-13, with that of Delageneste/Cheinisse from the Ecurie Savin-Calberson winning the Thermal Efficiency Index.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.224-27) The final finisher was the little Mini Marcos. Formerly the object of laughter, it had become a crowd favourite running like clockwork. As car after car ran into trouble and dropped out, the little Marcos, by this time nicknamed 'la puce bleue' (the blue flea) wailed on. Despite finishing 26 laps behind the rest of the field.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.233-26)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Moity_1974,_p.102-4-7) the car eventually came home at an incredible 15th overall.

It had taken three attempts for Ford to win [Indianapolis in '65](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Indianapolis_500 "1965 Indianapolis 500") and the NASCAR Championship, and now it added the Le Mans 24 Hours, with the Ford-[Cosworth DFV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosworth_DFV "Cosworth DFV") Formula One engine in development. Chrysler had first entered in 1925, and after these 41 years it was the first win for an American car.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clausager_1982,_p.147-31) The official [Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company") press release, dated July 5, 1966, claimed:

> The McLaren-Amon and the Miles-Hulme cars were running within seconds of each other as the race neared its end, with the Bucknum-Hutcherson car hanging back as insurance. A decision was made in the Ford pits to have the cars finish side by side in what hopefully would be considered a dead heat. All three cars went over the finish in formation, but any chance for a dead heat disappeared when officials discovered a rule that in case of a tie, the car that had started further down the grid had travelled the farther distance. Since McLaren and Amon had started 60 feet behind Miles and Hulme, they were declared the winners. Both [New Zealanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealanders "New Zealanders") who now reside in England, it was the most important victory yet for the two youngsters. McLaren, who builds his own Formula and sports cars, is 28. Amon 22, is the youngest winner in the history of the event. It was a record shattering performance as the winning car covered more miles (3,009.3) at a faster speed (125.38 mph) than any previous entry. It demonstrated that production engines could compete with racing powerplants and that an American-built car could top Europe's best.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-48)

The Ford team's decision was a big disappointment for Ken Miles, who was aiming for the '[endurance racing Triple Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_Crown_of_endurance_racing "Triple Crown of endurance racing")'—winning Daytona-Sebring-Le Mans—as a reward for his investment in the GT40 development. "I'm disappointed, of course, but what are you going to do about it."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-:0-49) Beebe also later admitted he had been annoyed with Miles racing Gurney, disregarding team orders by potentially risking the cars' endurance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15) Two months later, Ken Miles died at [Riverside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverside_International_Raceway "Riverside International Raceway") while testing the next generation Ford GT40 J-Car, which became the Mk IV that won Le Mans in 1967.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Spurring_2010,_p.210-3-15)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Fox_1973,_p.202-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-51)

In a race of attrition it was fortunate the big teams brought such quantity – only 3 of the 13 Fords finished, and only the two GTs finished from the 14 Ferraris entered. By contrast, 5 of the 7 Porsches finished (including their 911 in the GT class), as did four of the six Alpines, showing much better reliability. It was the first time that the 3000 miles/125 mph mark had been exceeded.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Clausager_1982,_p.147-31)

With the bitter failure of Ferrari's 330 P3 mirroring the failure of the Ford prototypes the previous year (and with salt rubbed into the wound with Ford's formation finish), the "Ford-Ferrari War" moved into its climactic phase. The Le Mans results boosted Ford over Ferrari for the [1966 Manufacturers' Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_World_Sportscar_Championship#Manufacturers'_Championship "1966 World Sportscar Championship"). Ford's answer to Ferrari's next weapon, the [330 P4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari_P "Ferrari P"), was delayed by development problems, handing Ferrari a rematch with the Mk IIs that so dominated them at Le Mans, at the 1967 [Daytona 24 Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytona_24_Hours "Daytona 24 Hours"). After a defective batch of transaxle shafts sank Ford's effort, Ferrari took a 1-2-3 finish with their new P4s and returned the favor of Ford's victory formation. Ford's [Mark IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40 "Ford GT40") was ready in time for the [12 Hours of Sebring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12_Hours_of_Sebring "12 Hours of Sebring"), where it won on its maiden outing. Three more examples were produced and prepared for the Le Mans 24 Hours, while Ford's championship hopes rested on the older [Ford GT40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40 "Ford GT40") and the new GT40-derived [Mirage M1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirage_(race_car) "Mirage (race car)") to gain points in the intervening races. After a disappointing showing at [Monza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000_km_Monza "1000 km Monza") and a controversial denial of championship points from a Mirage win at the [Spa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000_km_Spa "1000 km Spa") event, Ford saw limited opportunity for taking the Manufacturers' title again in 1967 and instead concentrated on a last hurrah at Le Mans, where the leading Mark IV, driven by Dan Gurney and A. J. Foyt, won handily. Ferrari took the Manufacturers' title for 1967, edging up-and-coming Porsche by two points.

The Ford-Ferrari War was ended by new rules for 1968 that eliminated large capacity engines as in the P4s and Mark IVs from eligibility for the Sports Prototype class with a 3-litre engine capacity limit, as in Formula One. The GT40 Mk.I already in 1966 had met the production requirement for [homologation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homologation_(motorsport) "Homologation (motorsport)") in the new [Group 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_4_(racing) "Group 4 (racing)") class, and fitted under the 5 litre limit for 1968. Ferrari found the production requirement for homologating the P4 under Group 4 daunting and withdrew from competition in the sport-racer classes. Neither Ford nor Ferrari fielded a factory team for the Manufacturers' Championship that year; however, the [John Wyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wyer "John Wyer") team running the Group 4 [Ford GT40 Mk.I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40_Mk.I "Ford GT40 Mk.I") with permitted updates brought home the title for Ford and in 1969 achieved wins with the GT40 at Sebring and a fourth time at Le Mans. When Ferrari was able to enter the homologated 512S car for 1970, the class they competed in was already dominated by the [Porsche 917](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche_917 "Porsche 917").

Several cars of the original 24-hours race have survived and have been restored to their former glory. The crowd-pleasing Mini Marcos was club raced, rallied and hill climbed, road registered twice and repainted five times only to be stolen in the night of 30 October 1975 from beneath a flat in Paris. Three days earlier Marcos-boss Harold Dermott had made a deal to buy the car with the intention to restore it and put on museum display. Several people searched for the car ever since, but it was only found back in December 2016 in Portugal by Dutchman Jeroen Booij.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Tom Kristensen has won the 24 Hours of Le Mans nine times, more than any other driver.

The 24 Hours of Le Mans (French: 24 Heures du Mans) is an annual 24-hour automobile endurance race organised by the automotive group Automobile Club de l'Ouest (ACO) and held on the Circuit de la Sarthe race track close to the city of Le Mans, the capital of the French department of Sarthe.[1][2] It was first held as the Grand Prix of Endurance and Efficiency in 1923,[3] after the automotive journalist Charles Faroux to Georges Durand, the ACO general secretary, and the industrialist Emile Coquile, agreed to hold the race for car manufacturers to test vehicle durability, equipment and reliability.[1] Each overall victor is presented with a trophy bearing the event's emblem and the logo of the ACO commissioned by the sporting director Jean-Pierre Moreau in 1993. All three-time consecutive winning manufacturers permanently keep the trophy.[4] Since 1991, at the initiative of a man named Bernard Warain,[5] a cast of the winning driver's feet, hands and signature are taken before the following year's race and put in a bronze car-wheel shaped plaque that is placed into the pavement in Le Mans' Saint Nicholas district.[6][7]

Tom Kristensen has won the event nine times, more than any other competitor. Jacky Ickx, the previous record holder, is second with six victories, and Derek Bell, Frank Biela and Emanuele Pirro are third with five wins each. Kristensen also achieved a record six victories in succession from the 2000 to the 2005 editions.[8] Hurley Haywood had the longest wait between his first Le Mans win and his last. He first won in 1977 and last won in 1994, a span of 17 years and 5 days. Alexander Wurz waited the longest between his inaugural victory at the 1996 event and his second win—following 12 years, 11 months, 29 days later—at the 2009 edition. Luigi Chinetti is the oldest Le Mans winner; he was 47 years, 11 months and 9 days old when he won the 1949 event. Wurz is the event's youngest winner; he was 22 years, 4 months and 1 day old when he won the 1996 race.[9] There have been a record 35 victors from the United Kingdom, followed by France with 28 and Germany with 18. A total of four countries have produced just one winner.[10]

Porsche have won the most races as a manufacturer with 19 since their first in 1970. Audi are second with 13 wins and Ferrari are third with 12 victories. Porsche also achieved the most consecutive wins with seven victories in succession from 1981 to 1987.[11] German manufacturers have won a record 34 times amongst four constructors, followed by the United Kingdom with 17 victories amongst 6 manufacturers and France with 15 wins amongst 9 constructors. Joest Racing are the most successful race team with 15 victories and the Audi R8 is the best race-winning vehicle with five victories.[10][12]

As of the 2026 24 Hours of Le Mans, there have been 153 victorious drivers from 24 individual countries and 25 winning manufacturers representing 7 different nations in the race's 94 editions. The first two winners were André Lagache and René Léonard in 1923, and the most recent drivers to achieve their first victory was Nyck de Vries in 2026. All years (except 1977, 1979 and 1983) until 1985 saw two drivers per entry win before three participants per car became the norm from 1985 onwards.[10] Timo Bernhard, Romain Dumas and Mike Rockenfeller set the record for the farthest distance covered by a race-winning team, driving 5,410.713 km (3,362.061 mi) and completing 397 laps in an Audi R15 TDI plus in 2010.[13] Frank Clement and John Duff hold the record for the shortest distance covered by a victorious squad, completing 120 laps and 2,077.34 km (1,290.80 mi) sharing a Bentley 3 Litre Sport in 1924.[14]

Notesedit
 While Canada had been independent since 1931, Canadians were deemed subjects of the United Kingdom until 1947.[14]
 Chinetti became an American citizen in 1946.[30]
 Ford decided to stage a photo finish and the ACO declared Amon and McLaren the 1966 winners because the duo began 20 metres (66 ft) away from their teammates Denny Hulme and Ken Miles.[48]
 John Winter was the pseudonym of gentleman driver Louis Krages.[72]
 The 1994 victory is listed with Porsche; Dauer Sportwagen was the official constructor of the road car, a Porsche 962 heavily modified for street use and race homologation.[82]
 The 1996 and 1997 victories are listed with Porsche, although the car was built by TWR on a modified Jaguar XJR-14 chassis, fitted with a Porsche 962 engine.[85][86]
 Ortelli is a French-born driver who is a citizen of Monaco.[90]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

34th 24 Hours of Le Mans endurance race

This article is about the race. For the 2019 film released internationally as _Le Mans '66_, see [_Ford v Ferrari_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_v_Ferrari "Ford v Ferrari").

1966 [24 Hours of Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "24 Hours of Le Mans")Previous: [1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "1965 24 Hours of Le Mans")Next: [1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "1967 24 Hours of Le Mans") Index: [Races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_races "Category:24 Hours of Le Mans races") | [Winners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans_winners "List of 24 Hours of Le Mans winners")

The **1966 [24 Hours of Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_of_Le_Mans "24 Hours of Le Mans")** was the 34th Grand Prix of Endurance, and took place on 18 and 19 June 1966.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-2) It was also the seventh round of the [1966 World Sportscar Championship season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_World_Sportscar_Championship_season "1966 World Sportscar Championship season"). This was the first overall win at Le Mans for the [Ford GT40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_GT40 "Ford GT40") as well as the first win for an American constructor in a major European race since [Jimmy Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Murphy_(racing_driver) "Jimmy Murphy (racing driver)")'s triumph with [Duesenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duesenberg "Duesenberg") at the [1921 French Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1921_French_Grand_Prix "1921 French Grand Prix").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_24_Hours_of_Le_Mans#cite_note-Sauber-3) It was also the debut Le Mans start for two significant drivers: [Henri Pescarolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Pescarolo "Henri Pescarolo"), who went on to set the record for the most starts at Le Mans; and [Jacky Ickx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacky_Ickx "Jacky Ickx"), whose record of six Le Mans victories stood until beaten by [Tom Kristensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kristensen_(racing_driver) "Tom Kristensen (racing driver)") in 2005.
